speaker: ALEX
text: Welcome back. Challenge 5 is called Make Your Mark, and this is where your Learning Room starts to feel like a real repository instead of a place you are only reading.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Because now we are changing an actual file, not just opening issues or looking around.

speaker: ALEX
text: Exactly. You will edit `docs/welcome.md`, replace a TODO with real content, and save that change with a commit message that says what changed and why. A commit is a saved snapshot in Git, so this is your first clear record of contribution.

speaker: JAMIE
text: And this happens in the private Learning Room repository that GitHub Classroom created for each learner, right? Not in the original template repository.

speaker: ALEX
text: Right. Your Learning Room is your own private copy from the classroom assignment, named something like `learning-room-your-username`. Everyone practices the same issue, branch, commit, pull request, review, and merge flow, but your work stays in your own repo unless facilitators intentionally arrange peer review. Day 1 prioritizes Challenges 1 through 6, so this one is part of the core path.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Before I touch the pencil icon, where should I be? I can imagine someone accidentally editing in the wrong place.

speaker: ALEX
text: Start in your Learning Room repository, then check the branch dropdown. For Challenge 5, you should be on your `learn/YOUR-USERNAME` branch, which is the practice branch you created earlier so your work is separate from `main`.

speaker: JAMIE
text: So the branch is a safety rail. I can make the change there first, and main stays stable.

speaker: ALEX
text: Yes. The Learning Room was designed for that kind of practice: safe enough to experiment, realistic enough to build real habits, and paced so you are not blocking anyone else.

speaker: JAMIE
text: What if someone is listening and thinking, I do not even see my Learning Room yet?

speaker: ALEX
text: Then go back to the GitHub Classroom assignment link, make sure you accepted the assignment, and open the repository link when GitHub finishes creating it. If Challenge 1 was missing earlier, the usual check was the Issues tab and then the Actions tab, where the progression workflow and Gandalf PR validation workflow live. By Challenge 5, you should already have that repo bookmarked and your challenge issue open.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Okay, what file are we editing?

speaker: ALEX
text: Open `docs/welcome.md`. The `docs` folder also contains practice files like `keyboard-shortcuts.md`, `setup-guide.md`, and `CHALLENGES.md`, but Challenge 5 is focused on the TODO you found earlier in the welcome file.

speaker: JAMIE
text: The issue says to replace the TODO with real content. Does that mean there is one correct sentence everyone has to use?

speaker: ALEX
text: No. The reference solution gives an example, not a required answer. For instance, it replaces a comment like `TODO: add link to workshop schedule` with a sentence that links to the workshop schedule file.

speaker: JAMIE
text: So if my TODO is about who can contribute, I write a clear sentence or two that actually belongs in that section.

speaker: ALEX
text: Exactly. Keep it small, useful, and related to the TODO. This is not a redesign of the whole page. It is one focused improvement.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Walk me through the browser version, because that is the path a lot of people will use first.

speaker: ALEX
text: In your Learning Room, confirm the branch dropdown says `learn/YOUR-USERNAME`. Then navigate to `docs/welcome.md`, open the file, and activate the pencil icon labeled `Edit this file`.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Then I find the TODO in the editor and replace it with my actual text.

speaker: ALEX
text: Yes. After the edit, move to the commit area. Write your commit message, and for this challenge commit directly to your `learn/YOUR-USERNAME` branch.

speaker: JAMIE
text: If I use a screen reader, is the pencil icon findable as a button?

speaker: ALEX
text: It should be. With NVDA or JAWS, many learners use button navigation to find `Edit this file`. With VoiceOver, the Buttons rotor can help. The important part is to verify the file name and branch before you start typing.

speaker: JAMIE
text: What if GitHub offers to create a new branch?

speaker: ALEX
text: For Challenge 5, stay with the challenge instruction and commit to your learning branch. In the next pull request work, you will see short-lived feature branches like `fix/yourname-issueXX`, but this challenge is about making one meaningful branch commit.

speaker: JAMIE
text: The commit message feels small, but it is doing a lot of work here.

speaker: ALEX
text: It is. A message like `Update welcome.md` tells us the file changed, but not what happened. A stronger message is `Add workshop description to welcome.md` or `Replace placeholder text with actual welcome message`.

speaker: JAMIE
text: So I should be able to read the message later and know the purpose of the change without reopening the file.

speaker: ALEX
text: That is the goal. A good commit message answers two plain questions: what changed, and why it changed.

speaker: JAMIE
text: The solution shows a more formal version too, right? Something like `docs: replace TODO with workshop schedule link`, then a short body underneath.

speaker: ALEX
text: Yes, and that format is useful. The first line is a short summary, often around 50 characters if you can manage it. Then a blank line can separate an optional body that explains the reason in more detail.

speaker: JAMIE
text: But I do not have to use the fancy prefix to pass the challenge.

speaker: ALEX
text: Correct. `Fix TODO in welcome.md` and `Add schedule link to welcome page` are both acceptable because they are clear. The convention is helpful, not mandatory.

speaker: JAMIE
text: After I commit, what evidence do I need to give back in the challenge issue?

speaker: ALEX
text: Paste the commit URL, share the exact commit message you used, and briefly say what you changed the TODO to say. The issue template asks for all three so a facilitator, bot, or future-you can follow the trail.

speaker: JAMIE
text: How do I find the commit URL if I have never copied one before?

speaker: ALEX
text: After the commit, GitHub usually shows the latest commit near the file or repository view. Open the commit message link, and copy the URL from the address bar. You can also use the commit history for the file if you need to find it again.

speaker: JAMIE
text: There is also a peer simulation check in the issue. What is that asking me to notice?

speaker: ALEX
text: Compare your commit message with the peer-simulation PR title and commit message in your repo. Ask yourself whether you can tell what changed just by reading the title or message. If you have a real buddy in the workshop, comparing messages is a good way to practice clarity without judging anyone's writing style.

speaker: JAMIE
text: What if the GitHub web editor is not the tool I want to use?

speaker: ALEX
text: That is fine. On github.com, the pencil icon path is the most direct. In github.dev, you can press `.` from the repository to open the browser-based VS Code editor, edit the file, and commit from Source Control.

speaker: JAMIE
text: And if I am working locally?

speaker: ALEX
text: You can use VS Code with Git: edit the file, stage with `git add`, and commit with `git commit`. GitHub Desktop works too: edit in your preferred editor, return to Desktop, write the message, and click Commit.

speaker: JAMIE
text: So the tool is flexible, but the outcome is not vague.

speaker: ALEX
text: Right. The successful outcome is a real edit in `docs/welcome.md` and a descriptive commit message saved on the correct branch.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Let us talk about the mistakes people are afraid of, because this is where anxiety can spike.

speaker: ALEX
text: The most common one is editing on `main` instead of your practice branch. If you catch it before committing, switch to `learn/YOUR-USERNAME` with the branch dropdown and make the edit there.

speaker: JAMIE
text: What if I cannot find the edit button at all?

speaker: ALEX
text: Look near the top-right area of the file view for the pencil icon, or search the buttons for `Edit this file`. If the button is unavailable, check that you are in your own Learning Room repo and signed in with the right GitHub account.

speaker: JAMIE
text: And the scary one: I accidentally committed to main.

speaker: ALEX
text: Ask your facilitator for help. It is fixable, and this is exactly why the Learning Room exists. You are practicing real work in a place where recovery is part of the lesson.

speaker: JAMIE
text: If I finished but I am not sure it is good enough, should I copy the solution exactly?

speaker: ALEX
text: Use the solution as a comparison, not as a script. Your edit can be different. Check that it replaces the TODO with real content, that the commit message makes sense, and that your evidence points to the commit.

speaker: JAMIE
text: How does this connect to pull requests? Challenge 5 is only a commit, but the chapter around it talks a lot about PRs.

speaker: ALEX
text: A pull request, or PR, is how a saved change becomes a proposed contribution for review and merge. Challenge 5 gives you the commit habit first, because every PR is made of commits.

speaker: JAMIE
text: So later, when I open a PR, the reviewer will see not only my description but also the commits behind it.

speaker: ALEX
text: Exactly. A PR page has several important places: the Conversation tab for the description, comments, and bot feedback; the Commits tab for saved changes; the Checks tab for automated results; and the Files changed tab for the diff.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Diff means the before-and-after view of the file, right?

speaker: ALEX
text: Yes. Removed lines and added lines are shown so reviewers can understand the change. In later PR work, you will also include a line like `Closes #XX` in the PR description so the related issue closes automatically when the PR is merged.

speaker: JAMIE
text: And Gandalf reads the PR too?

speaker: ALEX
text: Gandalf posts validation feedback on the PR Conversation tab. It can check things like issue linkage, description detail, and accessibility-related file issues. If something fails, you update the branch and the checks run again.

speaker: JAMIE
text: That makes the commit message part of a bigger communication chain.

speaker: ALEX
text: Yes. A clear commit helps the PR make sense, a clear PR helps review move faster, and review prepares you for contributing beyond the Learning Room.

speaker: JAMIE
text: There are a lot of moving pieces around the Learning Room: optional skills modules, peer review, bots, study groups. How much of that matters for this challenge?

speaker: ALEX
text: For Challenge 5, keep your attention on the edit and commit. But it helps to know the larger map: GitHub Skills modules are optional self-paced practice in your account, while the Learning Room is the required workshop track for Day 1.

speaker: JAMIE
text: And peers do not automatically see everything in my private repo.

speaker: ALEX
text: Right. Facilitators may arrange peer review or sharing when it is useful, but your repo is private by default. The usual PR flow is: you open a PR, automation gives feedback, a reviewer may comment, you respond or update, and then the work is merged when it is ready.

speaker: JAMIE
text: What if review takes a while, or I disagree with feedback?

speaker: ALEX
text: Ask for facilitator help, respond kindly, and keep the conversation tied to the change. Study groups are fine when the workshop allows them, but your evidence and decisions should still be your own.

speaker: JAMIE
text: It sounds like this tiny TODO edit is rehearsal for open source communication.

speaker: ALEX
text: It is. And if GitHub's interface changes, use current official GitHub documentation, GitHub's accessibility guidance, or your facilitator as references. The labels may move, but the workflow remains: find the right repo, use the right branch, make the smallest useful change, describe it clearly, and leave evidence someone else can follow.

speaker: JAMIE
text: So for Make Your Mark, I check my branch, edit `docs/welcome.md`, replace the TODO, commit with a meaningful message, paste the commit URL and message, and compare whether my message is understandable.

speaker: ALEX
text: That is the challenge. Small change, clear record, confident next step.

speaker: JAMIE
text: I like that. It is not about writing the perfect sentence. It is about making a real contribution that someone else can understand.
